procedural_history.originating_court: Sessions Judge, Tehri Garhwal in Sessions Trial No.7 of 1990
procedural_history.impugned_order: Final judgment and order dated 30.12.2009 passed by the High Court of Uttarakhand at Nainital in Criminal Appeal No.1644 of 2001 (Old No.2113/1996)
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The accused-appellants filed Criminal Appeal No.1644 of 2001 (Old No.2113/1996) in the High Court of Uttarakhand at Nainital challenging the order dated 11.10.1996 passed by the Sessions Judge, Tehri Garhwal in Sessions Trial No.7 of 1990. The High Court dismissed the appeal and confirmed the Sessions Judge's order.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The accused persons, aggrieved by the High Court's dismissal of their appeal, filed an appeal by way of special leave in the Supreme Court. During the pendency of the appeal in the Supreme Court, one of the accused (Rameshwar Singh (A-1)) expired, and the appeal against him abated. The Supreme Court ultimately dismissed the appeal.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court, in its appellate jurisdiction under Article 136, should re-appreciate evidence when there are concurrent findings of fact by two lower courts.

facts: Two lower courts had convicted the appellants based on their appreciation of the ocular and circumstantial evidence.
The appellants appealed to the Supreme Court under Article 136 of the Constitution.
The appellants' counsel argued that the concurrent findings of the lower courts were 'wholly perverse' and that it was a case of 'no evidence', urging the Supreme Court to re-examine the evidence.
law: The Supreme Court's general principle is that it will be 'very slow' to re-appreciate evidence in its appellate jurisdiction under Article 136 when there are concurrent findings of fact by two lower courts.
Quoting the case of Lachman Singh vs. State, the Court affirmed that its function is not to reassess evidence that has already been accepted by lower courts.

An exception to this principle exists if the appellant can demonstrate that the concurrent findings are 'wholly perverse', 'recorded without any evidence', or 'recorded by misreading or ignoring the material evidence'.
application: The Court first stated the established legal principle of its reluctance to interfere with concurrent findings of fact.

Despite this principle, the Court examined the evidence and the lower courts' findings to determine if any of the exceptions applied, specifically the appellants' claim of perversity and lack of evidence.
After reviewing the evidence related to motive, recovery of stolen articles, discovery of the weapon, and other circumstances, the Court found no reason to disbelieve or discard the evidence.
The Court concluded that the evidence was rightly believed by the two lower courts and that the prosecution had proven its case beyond a reasonable doubt.
Since the appellants failed to show that the findings were perverse or without evidence, the conditions for the exception were not met.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the request to re-appreciate the evidence. It held that while it has the power to do so, it will not interfere with concurrent findings of fact from two lower courts unless those findings are shown to be wholly perverse, without evidence, or based on a misreading of material evidence. In this case, the appellants failed to meet this high threshold, as the Court found the lower courts' appreciation of the evidence to be justified.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court, in its appellate jurisdiction under Article 136, should re-appreciate evidence when there are concurrent findings of fact by two lower courts.
appellant_arguments: The concurrent findings of the two lower courts are wholly “perverse” because they are based on evidence that is unreliable due to its poor quality and/or insufficiency.
The entire case is based on circumstantial evidence, and the prosecution failed to adduce sufficient evidence to prove the case beyond a reasonable doubt.
This is a case of no evidence against the appellants, making their conviction by the lower courts wholly unsustainable in law.
respondent_arguments: The conviction of the appellants should be supported.
The judgment of the lower courts does not call for any interference and the appeal should be dismissed.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When two lower courts have reached concurrent findings of fact based on an appreciation of evidence, the Supreme Court, in its appellate jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution, will not re-appreciate the evidence afresh unless the appellant can demonstrate that the findings are wholly perverse, recorded without any evidence, or are the result of misreading or ignoring material evidence.
obiter: It is not the function of this Court to reassess the evidence and an argument on a point of fact which did not prevail with the Courts below cannot avail the appellants in this Court.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court finds no merit in the appeal because it is unable to notice any perversity, arbitrariness, or illegality in the reasoning and conclusions of the two lower courts. The prosecution proved all circumstances with oral evidence beyond a reasonable doubt, which points the finger of guilt towards the appellants and establishes their complicity in the crime.
legal_tests_applied: When two lower courts have appreciated the entire ocular evidence, the Supreme Court, in its appellate jurisdiction under Article 136, will be very slow to appreciate the evidence afresh unless the appellants can demonstrate that the concurrent findings are wholly perverse, recorded without any evidence, or recorded by misreading or ignoring material evidence.
why_appellant_lost: The Court found no force in any of the submissions urged by the counsel for the appellants.
The appellants failed to demonstrate that the concurrent findings of the two lower courts were wholly perverse, arbitrary, or illegal.
Contrary to the appellants' claim that no motive was proved, the Court found no good reason to discard the evidence on motive, which was rightly believed by the two lower courts.
The Court found no reason to disbelieve or discard the evidence presented by the prosecution at the instance of the appellants.
why_respondent_won: The two lower courts, in their respective jurisdictions, had properly appreciated the entire ocular evidence.
The prosecution proved all circumstances with the aid of oral evidence beyond all reasonable doubt, which led to the commission of the crime and pointed the finger of guilt towards the appellants.
The reasoning and conclusions of the two lower courts were found to be free from any perversity, arbitrariness, or illegality.
policy_considerations: The Supreme Court should be very slow in exercising its appellate jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution to appreciate evidence afresh when there are concurrent findings of fact by two lower courts, unless specific and severe flaws like perversity or lack of evidence are pointed out.
